# Isaiah 11: Verse-by-verse research notes

**Before you use these notes:**
- I couldn't find enough on some things you asked for. I found nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings of this chapter. I found no Orthodox source beyond one Church Father, Gregory Nazianzen. I found no Bible Odyssey article. Verse 15 is thinly covered.
- The Hoekema page on monergism.com only loaded partway. I could read just its opening part on Isaiah 11, so I've only reported that part.
- I didn't fetch the Enduring Word page for verses 13–16 in full. For those verses I've used Guzik's study guide on blueletterbible.org instead.
- About the commentators' traditions: the site labels Barnes as Presbyterian and Keil & Delitzsch as Lutheran. The other labels (Calvin, Henry and Hoekema as Reformed; Wesley as Methodist) are well known, but the pages I read don't state them. Please check them.

---

**v. 1**
- **Traditional reading:**
  - Calvin says the verse comforts godly people who would otherwise despair after the terrible disasters just described. As the description of such dreadful calamities might terrify the godly, and give them reason for despair, it was necessary to hold out consolation — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/11-1.html
  - Calvin also says the verse applies solely to the person of Christ. It can't mean Hezekiah or Josiah, because both were raised from infancy expecting to be king. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/11-1.html
  - Poole makes a similar point about Hezekiah. Hezekiah was already born when Isaiah gave this prophecy, so it must refer to someone not yet born: the Messiah. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/11-1.htm
  - The Pulpit Commentary says "the stem of Jesse" must mean David's royal house, since Scripture has only one Jesse. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/11-1.html
- **Guzik (Enduring Word):**
  - Isaiah 10:33–34 pictured God cutting down proud nations like trees. Here God makes a shoot grow from one of the stumps: Jesse's family. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-11/
  - David's royal authority had lain dormant for about 600 years when Jesus came. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-11/
  - Saying "from Jesse" instead of "from King David" stresses how humble the Messiah's origin would be. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-11/
- **Keil & Delitzsch (Lutheran):** the world's great empire falls with no hope once the axe strikes it, But in Israel spring is returning. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/11-1.html
- **Ligonier (Reformed):** David's dynasty nearly died out when God judged his people through Assyria and Babylon. But a barely visible shoot would grow into a mighty tree. — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/shoot-jesses-stump
- **Precept Austin (dispensational):** reads the stump as the believing remnant of David's family. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah_11_commentary
- **Modern scholarship (NET Bible notes):**
  - Isaiah may name Jesse rather than David to suggest a new David, not just another disappointing Davidic descendant. — https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Isa&chapter=11
  - Text note: the ancient translations, and the parallel lines of the poem, suggest the original word was "will sprout" rather than "will bear fruit." — https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Isa&chapter=11
  - The Precept Austin page mentions in passing that some interpreters think Hezekiah or Josiah is meant, and answers them from 2 Thessalonians 2:8. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/60575/

**v. 2**
- **Traditional reading:**
  - Barnes (Presbyterian) says this is the Holy Spirit, the third person of the Trinity, coming on the Messiah in full. "Rest" means the Spirit stays permanently, not just for a moment. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/11-2.html
  - The Pulpit Commentary says Jesus' human nature needed, and received in full, the Spirit's work of making holy and giving light. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/11.htm
- **Keil & Delitzsch (Lutheran):** count seven "spirits," ordered like the seven-branched lampstand. The Spirit of the LORD is the central shaft, and the three pairs are its branches. The fear of the LORD is the foundation of all the rest. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/11-2.htm
- **Guzik:** the seven aspects show the Spirit's fullness and lie behind the "seven spirits" of Revelation 1:4. He stresses that Jesus ministered as a Spirit-filled man, relying on the Spirit rather than on His own divine resources. As God, Jesus always had these qualities. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-11/
- **Where traditions differ: are there seven gifts or six?**
  - **Calvin (Reformed):** the verse is about Christ's human nature. Christ received the Spirit's gifts so that He could give them to us. Calvin calls the Catholic doctrine of "sevenfold grace" a mistake: the verse lists only six, and a seventh was invented. He adds that Scripture describes many more gifts than seven. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/11-2.html
  - **Catholic view:** Catholic tradition names seven gifts: wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety and fear of God. Isaiah 11:1–3 is the only place in the Bible where the seven are listed together. — https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/the-seven-gifts-of-the-holy-spirit
  - Thomas Aquinas uses this verse as his authority for listing counsel and knowledge among the gifts. — https://www.newadvent.org/summa/3052.htm and https://www.newadvent.org/summa/3009.htm
  - Where the seventh gift comes from: the Douay-Rheims (Catholic) translation and the Greek Septuagint both include "godliness." — https://biblehub.com/isaiah/11-2.htm
  - **Church Father:** Gregory Nazianzen calls these seven precious spirits. He thinks Isaiah calls the Spirit's activities "spirits." — https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/310241.htm
  - **GotQuestions** counts seven by including "the Spirit of the LORD" itself. — https://www.gotquestions.org/seven-spirits-God.html
- **Modern scholarship (NET Bible notes):**
  - Like David (1 Samuel 16:13), this king is empowered by the Spirit. — https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Isa&chapter=11
  - The qualities come as three pairs. "Counsel and strength" means the ability to carry out plans. "Knowledge and fear of the LORD" together mean loyalty to God. — https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Isa&chapter=11

**v. 3**
- **Meaning of "delight":** the Hebrew literally says "his smelling," that is, taking pleasure the way one enjoys incense. Some scholars think the line was accidentally repeated by a copyist and should be dropped (NET Bible notes). — https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Isa&chapter=11
- **Guzik's link to "smell":** he says the Hebrew for "understanding" in v. 2 suggests a keen sense of smell. He quotes Trapp: Jesus "smells out" a hypocrite. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-11/
- **Pulpit Commentary:** the King James rendering "of quick understanding" isn't supported by other uses of the word. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/11.htm
- **Guzik, quoted by Precept Austin:** human kings must rely on appearances and words, which can mislead. The Messiah sees hearts and can tell when people are lying or pretending. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/60575/

**v. 4**
- **Ligonier:** Jesus is greater than David because He judges the poor rightly. He alone can make sure the least of people get perfect justice. — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/shoot-jesses-stump
- **Wesley (Methodist):** the "rod" is Christ's word, His royal sceptre. Through its preaching He won the world, and He will destroy His enemies by it (2 Thessalonians 2:8). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/isaiah-11.html
- **Guzik:** Paul probably had this verse in mind in 2 Thessalonians 2:8. Paul applied to Jesus words Isaiah used of the LORD (Yahweh). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-thessalonians-2/
- **Where readings differ: when is this fulfilled?**
  - Guzik cites a writer who applies "the wicked" to the Antichrist. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-11/
  - Matthew Henry notes that the Aramaic paraphrase reads "the wicked" as Rome. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_011.cfm
  - Chuck Smith (dispensational) refers the verse to the Second Coming. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/11-2.html
  - Hoekema (Reformed, amillennial) notes that even the dispensational scholar Walvoord admits "the rod of his mouth" is figurative. — https://www.monergism.com/amillennialism
- **Modern scholarship (NET Bible notes):** some scholars change "earth" to "tyrant" so the lines match better, but the note says this may not be needed. "Breath of his lips" means his official decrees. — https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Isa&chapter=11

**v. 5**
- **Matthew Henry:** righteousness will cling to Him like a belt, as both His ornament and His strength. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_011.cfm
- **Wesley:** a belt was both an ornament and a sign of power. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/isaiah-11.html
- **Pulpit Commentary:** compares Ephesians 6:14. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/11.htm
- **NET Bible notes:** the word could mean an outer belt or an undergarment, and the exact point of the picture is uncertain. — https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Isa&chapter=11

**vv. 6–8** (the main point of disagreement)
- **Literal future renewal of creation:**
  - Guzik: nature will be transformed and animals may all become plant-eaters (Romans 8:19–22). Many think people will be vegetarian in the Millennium. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-11/
  - Bible.org (premillennial): the curse will be lifted. — https://bible.org/seriespage/chapter-3-return-christ-premillennial
  - Precept Austin: a literal change in animal diets is not hard to believe. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/60575/
  - Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: the animals may stand for kinds of people, but a literal return to Eden is a more likely interpretation. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/11-6.htm
- **Spiritual reading, the gospel changing people:**
  - Matthew Henry: when Paul, who had persecuted Christians, joined them, the wolf lived with the lamb. Some hope for a further fulfilment in the last days. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_011.cfm
  - Barnes: the language is poetic, like ancient "golden age" pictures. The gospel changes fierce human passions "as if" the animals had changed. Vitringa read the animals as enemies of the cross. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/11-6.html
  - A sermon on Bible Hub rejects putting centuries between the parts of this prophecy. It argues the peace began when Christ came. — https://biblehub.com/sermons/isaiah/11-6.htm
- **Wesley (Methodist) holds both:** animals restored to their state before the Fall, and cruel people made gentle by grace. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/isaiah-11.html
- **Hoekema (Reformed, amillennial):** a future earthly Millennium is by no means the only possible one reading. He points instead to the new earth (Isaiah 65:17; Revelation 21:1). — https://www.monergism.com/amillennialism
- **Constable:** amillennial interpreters do not expect a future earthly reign of the Messiah. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-11.html
- **Details:**
  - Pulpit Commentary: these were the only fierce animals in Palestine. A child leading them shows people's authority over animals increased. Lions eating straw isn't impossible. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/11.htm
  - Ellicott: possibly allegorical. He notes a parallel in Virgil's Fourth Eclogue. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/11-6.htm
- **Modern scholarship (NET Bible notes):** the animal picture stands for human society under a just king, where the categories of oppressor and oppressed vanish. — https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Isa&chapter=11

**v. 9**
- **Pulpit Commentary:** "holy mountain" is the name for the Messiah's church, taken from Zion. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/11.htm
- **Matthew Henry:** the knowledge of God ends people's hostility. Through the gospel, knowledge of God spreads beyond Judah to everyone. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_011.cfm
- **Guzik:** "knowledge" here means knowing God personally, not just intellectually. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-11/
- **Preacher's Homiletical Commentary:** like the sea, which is evenly full everywhere, this knowledge will reach everyone. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/11-1.html
- **NET Bible notes:** "knowledge of the LORD" means recognising His rule and submitting to it. Notes on vv. 4 and 9 add that it is unclear whether the scene covers the whole world or the land of Israel. — https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Isa&chapter=11

**v. 10**
- **Matthew Henry:** Paul applies this verse in Romans 15:12, which is the key to the prophecy. Christ is the banner lifted up on the cross (John 12:32). Henry lists views of "his rest": Christ's death, His ascension, or (Henry's preference) the church. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_011.cfm
- **Calvin:** the Gentiles, who once despised the Jews, will bow to their King. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/11-10.html
- **Clarke:** John takes "root" from this verse in Revelation 5:5 and 22:16. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/11-10.html
- **Different renderings of "glorious rest" (Barnes):** the Aramaic paraphrase reads it as his royal residence. The Latin Vulgate, the Bible traditionally used by Catholics, reads "his sepulchre shall be glorious." — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/11-10.html
- **Guzik:** in Isaiah 5:26 the banner called nations to bring judgment. Here it calls them to blessing. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-11/

**v. 11**
- **What was the "first time"?**
  - Wesley: the return from Babylon, so the second gathering happens in the Messiah's days. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/isaiah-11.html
  - Jennings (quoted on Precept Austin): v. 16 shows it was the Exodus from Egypt. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/60575/
  - NET Bible notes: also links it to the Exodus, and says the Hebrew is grammatically incomplete here. — https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Isa&chapter=11
- **Where readings differ: the church, or future national Israel?**
  - Clarke: this certainly remains yet to be accomplished. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/11-11.html
  - Guzik: a new Exodus of the Jewish people from all nations in the Messiah's reign. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-11/
  - Calvin: this is how God restores the church. He notes Jews had fled to Egypt, Ethiopia and other lands. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/11-11.html
  - Matthew Henry: fulfilled when Jews of the Dispersion came to Christ (James 1:1). — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_011.cfm
  - John Piper (Desiring God): stresses that the focus is on the remnant of Israel scattered among the nations. — https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-shoot-from-jesse-the-nations-and-israel

**v. 12**
- **Pulpit Commentary:** Christ is the banner. "Outcasts" is a masculine word and "dispersed" a feminine one, so the verse means both men and women of Israel and Judah. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/11.htm
- **Precept Austin:** links Isaiah 49:22, where Gentiles bring Israelites home. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/60575/

**v. 13**
- **Matthew Henry:** the old feud between Ephraim and Judah will end, and they will unite against common enemies. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_011.cfm
- **NET Bible notes:** "adversaries of Judah" normally means Judah's enemies. But the context suggests Judah's own hostility toward Ephraim. — https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Isa&chapter=11

**v. 14**
- **Spiritual reading:**
  - Pulpit Commentary: actual war is not meant. The neighbouring nations stand for the church's enemies, fought with legitimate weapons. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/11.htm
  - Wesley: the spiritual victory Christ wins through His apostles and ministers. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/isaiah-11.html
- **Literal future reading (Precept Austin):** a reunited Israel under the Messiah will be the dominant political power in the world. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/60575/
- **NET Bible notes:** "swoop" pictures a bird of prey. "Philistines' slopes" means the hills west of Judah. — https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Isa&chapter=11

**v. 15**
- **Pulpit Commentary:** physical obstacles will not stop the exiles from returning. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/11.htm
- **Matthew Henry:** when God's time comes, mountains of opposition become plains. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_011.cfm
- **Precept Austin:** links the drying of the Red Sea in Exodus 14:21–22. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/60575/

**v. 16**
- **Guzik:** every obstacle to gathering the scattered will be removed, because nothing can oppose the Messiah's rule. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/isaiah/isaiah-11.cfm
- **Matthew Henry:** expects God to gather His ancient people and bring in the full number of the Gentiles. He urges readers to walk the "highway of holiness." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/isaiah/11.htm
- **Jennings:** the first Exodus is the pattern for this future one from every country. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/60575/
